chapters.title: Board, setup and how the pieces move
Defence, king safety and escaping threats
Positional play, pawn structure and strong squares
Endgames, king activity, promotion and opposition

lessons.title: The board and its squares
objectives: Name any square, like e4
Find files, ranks and diagonals

steps.say: Welcome to Chackmate. The board has 64 squares in 8 columns and 8 rows. The light square is always in the bottom-right corner.
Columns are called files and are lettered a to h. Rows are called ranks and are numbered 1 to 8. White starts on ranks 1 and 2.
Every square has a name: its file, then its rank. This glowing square is e4, one of the four centre squares.
Squares of the same colour that touch at the corners form a diagonal, like this one from a1 to h8.

exercises.prompt: Click the e4 square.
hints: Files are letters, ranks are numbers.
Find the e-file, then count up 4.

exercises.prompt: Click d5.
hints: d is the fourth file from the left.
Count up five rows.

exercises.prompt: Click any one of the four centre squares.
hints: They are in the very middle of the board.

exercises.prompt: Click h8, the top-right corner from White's side.
hints: The h-file is on the right, rank 8 is at the far end.

lessons.title: Setting up the pieces
objectives: Set up the starting position
Remember: queen on her own colour

steps.say: This is the starting position. Pawns fill the second rank. Rooks go in the corners, then knights, then bishops.
The queen goes on her own colour: the white queen on the light square d1, the black queen on the dark square d8. The kings stand next to them.
White always moves first. After that, the players take turns, one move each.

exercises.prompt: The white queen is missing. Click the square where she starts.
hints: The queen goes on her own colour.
The white queen is on a light square on rank 1.

exercises.prompt: Click the black king.
hints: The king stands next to the queen.
Look on rank 8, the e-file.

exercises.prompt: White's knights are missing. Click a square where one starts.
hints: Knights stand next to the rooks.

exercises.prompt: Black's bishops are missing. Click a square where one starts.
hints: Bishops stand next to the king and queen.

lessons.title: The rook, bishop, queen and king
objectives: Move rooks, bishops and the queen along their lines
Move the king one square at a time

steps.say: The rook moves in straight lines, up, down and sideways, as far as it likes until something is in the way.
The bishop moves diagonally, any distance. A bishop that starts on a light square stays on light squares all game.
Pieces cannot jump over others. They can capture an enemy piece by landing on its square.
The queen is the strongest piece. She moves like a rook and a bishop combined.
The king is the most important piece but moves only one square in any direction. Lose the king and you lose the game.

exercises.prompt: Click every square the rook on c3 can move to.
hints: Straight lines only.
Four directions: up, down, left and right.

exercises.prompt: Now every square the bishop on e5 can reach.
hints: Diagonals only.
Your own pawn on b2 is in the way.

exercises.prompt: Capture the black pawn with your rook.
hints: The pawn is on the same file as your rook.

exercises.prompt: Click every square the queen on e3 can reach.
hints: Rook lines plus bishop lines.
Eight directions in total.

exercises.prompt: Click every safe square for the king on e2.
hints: One square in any direction.
The rook guards the whole third rank.

lessons.title: The knight's jump
objectives: Move the knight in an L shape
Use the knight's ability to jump

steps.say: The knight moves in an L: two squares one way, then one square to the side. It always lands on a square of the other colour.
The knight is the only piece that can jump over others. That is why it can leave the back rank at the very start of the game.
On the edge a knight reaches fewer squares, and in a corner only two. Knights are happiest near the centre.

exercises.prompt: Click every square the knight on e5 can jump to.
hints: Two squares, then one to the side.
There are eight of them from the centre.

exercises.prompt: A knight in the corner is much weaker. Click its squares.
hints: Only two squares are possible from a corner.

exercises.prompt: Jump over the pawns and develop the g1 knight towards the centre.
hints: The centre is d4, e4, d5 and e5.
Nf3 points the knight at e5 and d4.

wrong.g1h3: That works, but a knight on the edge controls fewer squares. Aim for the centre.

exercises.prompt: Use your knight to capture the rook.
hints: Two squares one way, then one to the side.

lessons.title: Pawns, promotion and en passant
objectives: Move pawns forward and capture diagonally
Promote a pawn on the last rank
Capture en passant

steps.say: Pawns move straight forward one square. From their starting square they may move two.
Pawns capture differently: one square diagonally forward. They never move backwards.
When a pawn reaches the far end it promotes. You choose a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Almost always, choose a queen.
If a pawn moves two squares and lands right beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only one. This is en passant, French for 'in passing'.
You can only do it on the very next move. Wait one turn and the chance is gone.

exercises.prompt: Click every square this pawn can move to.
hints: From its first square a pawn can move one or two.

exercises.prompt: Capture the knight with your pawn.
hints: Pawns capture diagonally forward.

exercises.prompt: Promote your pawn to a queen.
hints: Push the pawn to the last rank and choose the queen.

exercises.prompt: White just played c2 to c4. Capture en passant.
hints: Your pawn moves diagonally to c3.
The white pawn on c4 is removed.

lessons.title: Capturing and piece values
objectives: Use piece values to compare trades
Pick the most valuable safe capture

steps.say: A rough guide to value: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king is priceless.
When you have a choice of captures, take the most valuable piece you can win safely.
A piece is defended when one of its friends could take back. Grab a defended pawn with your queen, and you lose the queen.

exercises.prompt: Which capture wins the most? Play it.
hints: A rook is worth 5, a pawn 1.

wrong.d3b5: The pawn is only worth 1. The rook on h7 is worth 5.

exercises.prompt: You can trade your bishop for a rook. Is that good for you?
options: Yes: a rook (5) is worth more than a bishop (3)

exercises.prompt: Two captures, but only one is safe. Take it.
hints: Which black piece has no defender?

wrong.d1d5: The pawn on e6 takes back, and your queen is lost for a knight.

exercises.prompt: You trade your knight for a bishop. Who gains?

lessons.title: Check and its three escapes
objectives: Recognise check
Escape by moving, blocking or capturing

steps.say: When a king is attacked, it is in check. You must get out of check immediately.
There are three ways out: move the king, block the attack, or capture the attacker. Remember them as run, block, take.
A knight check cannot be blocked, because the knight jumps. Run with the king, or take the knight.

exercises.prompt: Your king is in check. Move it to safety.
hints: The rook controls the whole first rank.
Step up, off the rank.

exercises.prompt: Block the check with your bishop.
hints: Put a piece between the rook and your king. Your knight on e2 will defend it.
The bishop can reach c1.

exercises.prompt: Capture the piece giving check.
hints: The rook is right next to your king and nothing defends it.

exercises.prompt: A knight gives check. Take it.
hints: A knight check cannot be blocked.
Your pawn can capture it.

lessons.title: Checkmate and the first mates
objectives: Recognise checkmate
Deliver simple mates in one
Mate with two rooks

steps.say: Checkmate is check with no escape. The king cannot run, the check cannot be blocked and the attacker cannot be captured. Checkmate wins the game.
This pattern is called the back-rank mate: the king's own pawns trap it.
Two rooks checkmate by taking turns: one guards a rank, the other gives check on the next rank. The king is pushed to the edge like climbing a ladder.

exercises.prompt: Checkmate in one move.
hints: Black's king is stuck behind its pawns.
Use the rook on the back rank.

exercises.prompt: Checkmate with the queen.
hints: Your king already covers g7 and h7.
Attack along the eighth rank.

wrong.b1h1: Black escapes to g8. Check along the eighth rank instead.

exercises.prompt: Finish the ladder: checkmate in one.
hints: The a7 rook already guards the seventh rank.
Give check on the eighth.

wrong.a7a8: The king escapes to the seventh rank. Keep the a7 rook where it is.

exercises.prompt: Rook and king: checkmate in one.
hints: Your king takes away c7, d7 and e7.
Check along the back rank.

lessons.title: Castling rules
objectives: Castle on either side
Know when castling is not allowed

steps.say: Castling is a special move of the king and a rook. The king moves two squares towards the rook, and the rook jumps over to the other side of the king.
You may not castle if the king or that rook has moved, if you are in check, or if the king would pass through or land on an attacked square.
Castling queenside, the king goes to c1 and the rook to d1. The b1 square may be attacked: only the squares the king crosses must be safe.

exercises.prompt: Castle on the kingside.
hints: Move your king two squares towards the h1 rook.

exercises.prompt: Castle on the queenside.
hints: Move your king two squares towards the a1 rook.

exercises.prompt: The black rook attacks f1, so you cannot castle kingside. Castle the other way.
hints: The queenside path, d1 and c1, is safe.

exercises.prompt: Your king is in check. Can you castle out of it?
options: No: you may not castle while in check

lessons.title: Stalemate and other draws
objectives: Recognise stalemate
Avoid stalemating when winning
Know the ways a game can be drawn

steps.say: If the side to move has no legal moves but is not in check, it is stalemate, and the game is a draw. Even a queen up!
When you are winning, always check that your opponent still has a move, unless you are delivering checkmate.
A game is drawn by stalemate, by agreement, when neither side has enough pieces to checkmate, or when the same position appears three times.
There is also the fifty-move rule: fifty moves each with no capture and no pawn move, and a player may claim a draw.

exercises.prompt: Win with checkmate. Careful not to stalemate.
hints: Your king protects g7.
Put the queen next to the black king.

wrong.g1g6: Stalemate! Black has no moves but is not in check. That is only a draw.

exercises.prompt: Black to move has no legal moves and is not in check. What is the result?
King and bishop against a lone king. Can the bishop side win?
options: No, it is a draw: not enough material

exercises.prompt: The same position has appeared three times. What can a player do?

lessons.title: The centre and development
objectives: Occupy or control the centre early
Bring knights and bishops out
Value tempo in the opening

steps.say: Pieces in the centre control more squares and can switch quickly to either side. Start by placing a pawn in the centre.
1. e4 opens lines for the queen and bishop and grabs central space.
Developing means bringing pieces off the back rank. Knights first, usually towards the centre, then bishops.
Every move in the opening is precious. Moving one piece again and again leaves the others asleep at home.

exercises.prompt: Make a first move that puts a pawn in the centre.
hints: The centre squares are d4, e4, d5 and e5.

wrong.a2a4: Edge pawns do little at the start. Aim for the centre.

exercises.prompt: White took the centre. Answer by challenging it with a pawn.
hints: A pawn on e5 or d5 contests the centre directly.

exercises.prompt: Develop a knight towards the centre.
hints: Knights belong on f3 and c3.

exercises.prompt: Now develop your light-squared bishop to an active square.
hints: c4 aims at f7, b5 pressures the knight on c6.

exercises.prompt: Your knight is already on f3. What usually helps more on the next move?
Develop a new piece rather than moving the f3 knight again.
hints: Your b1 knight and f1 bishop have not moved yet.

lessons.title: Castle early, chase the queen
objectives: Castle early to protect the king
Defend against early queen attacks
Finish development by connecting rooks

steps.say: A king in the centre is exposed once lines open. Castling tucks it away and brings a rook towards the middle.
An early queen can be chased by developing moves, gaining you time. But first, deal with any threat!
Development is complete when the rooks see each other along the back rank. Then they can move to the open files.

exercises.prompt: Your pieces are out. Make your king safe.
hints: The squares between your king and the h1 rook are empty.

exercises.prompt: White threatens Qxf7 checkmate. Stop it.
hints: Block the f-file or defend f7.
Nf6 blocks the queen and develops a piece.

wrong.g7g6: That does not block the f-file. Qxf7 is still checkmate.

exercises.prompt: Black's queen came out early. Develop a piece that attacks it.
hints: A knight can attack h4 and develop at the same time.

exercises.prompt: What connects your rooks?
options: Moving all pieces off the back rank between them

lessons.title: Early traps and a model opening
objectives: Spot the fastest mates
Avoid weakening the king early
Play a sound opening from start to castling

steps.say: Moving the f and g pawns early opens a diagonal to the white king. This is the fastest checkmate in chess, the Fool's Mate.
At the start, f7 is Black's weakest square and f2 is White's: only the king defends them. Early attacks often aim there.
Watch a model opening: centre pawn, knights out, bishop active, castle.

exercises.prompt: Punish White's weak pawn moves: checkmate in one.
hints: The e1–h4 diagonal is open.
Your queen can reach h4.

exercises.prompt: Black left f7 weak. Checkmate!
hints: f7 is only defended by the king.
Your bishop supports the queen.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Develop and prepare to castle.
hints: Your g8 knight is the last minor piece at home.

exercises.prompt: Why is the Fool's Mate so fast?
options: White weakened the king with f3 and g4
Black's queen is the strongest piece

lessons.title: Forks and double attacks
objectives: Attack two pieces with one move
Use checks that hit a second target

steps.say: A fork is one piece attacking two or more targets at once. Knights are famous forkers.
After Nc7 check, the king must move, and the rook on a8 falls.
The queen moves in eight directions, so a single queen move can attack two things at once. A check plus an attack is the strongest kind: the opponent must deal with the check first.

Queen to a4 is check along the diagonal and attacks the knight on h4 along the rank. Black answers the check and the knight falls. Note the target: a rook on h4 could simply capture the queen back along the rank.

exercises.prompt: Fork the king and queen.
hints: Find a knight check that also attacks the queen.

exercises.prompt: Win the knight with a double attack.
hints: Look for a queen check.
The check should also line up with the knight.

exercises.prompt: Find the fork.
Find the fork.
Find the fork.

lessons.title: Pins and skewers
objectives: Pin a piece to something more valuable
Win the piece behind a more valuable one

steps.say: A pin attacks a piece that cannot move without exposing something more valuable behind it. Pinned to the king, it cannot move at all.
A pin to the king is absolute: the piece may not move at all. A pin to a queen or rook is relative: it may move, but it costs material.
A skewer is a pin in reverse: the valuable piece is in front. It must move, and the piece behind it is lost.

exercises.prompt: Pin the knight to the king.
hints: Line up your bishop with the knight and the king.

exercises.prompt: Skewer the king and win the rook.
hints: Check the king along a diagonal.
The rook is on the same diagonal, behind the king.

exercises.prompt: Use the pin.
Find the skewer or the winning line.
Find the skewer or the winning line.
Find the skewer or the winning line.

lessons.title: Discoveries, loose pieces and defenders
objectives: Move one piece to unleash another
Spot undefended pieces
Lure a defender away

steps.say: When a piece moves out of the way of a rook, bishop or queen, it can uncover an attack. If the moving piece also attacks something, the opponent faces two threats.
Loose pieces drop off. Before every move, ask: what is undefended, mine and theirs?
A defender that guards two things is overloaded. Here the rook on e8 is Black's only guard of the back rank. It must stay on the e-file: if it is ever lured away, White's rook lands on e8 with mate.
Deflection is the same idea from the other side: you force a defender to leave its post, often with a capture or a check it must answer, then strike at what it was guarding.

exercises.prompt: Uncover the attack.
Uncover the attack.
Win material.
Win material.
A black knight defends both a rook and a bishop. What is the most direct way to exploit it?
options: Attack the knight or one of the pieces it defends
Ignore it and push a pawn
exercises.explain: An overloaded piece cannot answer two threats. Capture one of the things it guards, and when it recaptures, the other is undefended.

lessons.title: Mating patterns and the tactics checklist
objectives: Recognise common mates
Check every forcing move before you decide

steps.say: Back-rank mates, smothered mates and queen-and-bishop batteries appear again and again. Recognising them saves calculation.
The smothered mate: the king is boxed in by its own pieces, and a knight gives the final check.
Most tactics are found by one habit: before every move, look at all checks, then all captures, then all threats. For both sides.
Forcing moves limit your opponent's answers, which makes them easy to calculate. That is why strong players look at them first.

exercises.prompt: Smothered mate: checkmate with the knight.
hints: The king is hemmed in by its own rook and pawns.
Jump to f7.

exercises.prompt: Queen and bishop: checkmate in one.
hints: Your queen and bishop line up on h7.
Capture on h7.

exercises.prompt: In what order should you scan for forcing moves?
exercises.explain: Checks leave the fewest replies, captures change material, threats force a response. Scan them in that order.

exercises.prompt: Checkmate!
Checkmate!

lessons.title: Seeing threats and escaping attacks
objectives: Ask what your opponent wants after every move
Move, defend, block or counter-attack

steps.say: Defence starts with one question after every opponent move: what does that move threaten? Look at their checks, captures and threats just as you look at your own.
Here Black has just played knight to c6, attacking your queen. If you miss it, you lose the queen for a knight.
When a piece is attacked you have four choices: move it, defend it, block the attack, or create a bigger threat of your own.
Moving is usually simplest for valuable pieces. Defending works when the attacker is worth more than what it attacks.

exercises.prompt: Your queen is attacked. Move it to a safe square.
hints: The knight on c3 attacks d5.
Pick a square no white piece attacks.

exercises.prompt: Your knight is attacked by a pawn. Save it.
hints: The pawn on e5 attacks f6.
Move the knight to a square no pawn attacks.

exercises.prompt: Your opponent moves a bishop next to your king. What do you check first?
options: Whether it gives check or threatens a capture

exercises.prompt: A pawn attacks your rook. Which defence is usually worst?
options: Defending the rook with another piece
Moving the rook to an open file
exercises.explain: A pawn is worth less than a rook, so defending the rook does not help: the pawn still wins the exchange. Move the rook instead.

lessons.title: Blocking checks and back-rank safety
objectives: Interpose a piece to stop a check
Give your king an escape square in time

steps.say: A check along a line can be blocked by putting a piece in between. Here Black's rook checks along the first rank.
Your king has no squares: its own pawns hem it in. Blocking with a defended piece is the only way out.
A castled king behind three unmoved pawns has no escape square. A single rook or queen check on the back rank can be mate.
A quiet pawn move such as h3 or g3, called making luft, gives the king a square and removes the danger.

exercises.prompt: Block the check.
hints: Put a piece on the first rank between the rook and your king.
Make sure the blocking piece is defended: on e1 the queen would be lost with mate.

wrong.e2e1: The rook takes on e1 with checkmate: nothing defends that square.

exercises.prompt: Why could your king not just step away?
options: Its own pawns block every escape square
Kings cannot move when in check

exercises.prompt: Show the danger: checkmate on the back rank.
hints: Black's king cannot move up.
A rook check on the eighth rank is mate.

exercises.prompt: Which move gives your castled king on g1 an escape square?

lessons.title: Counter-attacks, forks and defensive trades
objectives: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
Keep pieces off forkable squares
Trade the attacker's best pieces

steps.say: Sometimes the best defence is a stronger threat. If your opponent must answer your check or save their queen, they never get to carry out their own threat.
Be careful: a counter-attack only works if it is really bigger. A threat against a pawn does not answer a threat against your queen.
Knight forks are easiest to prevent before they happen. Look for squares where an enemy knight would attack two of your pieces or your king and a piece.
If your king and rook sit a knight's fork apart, move one of them or cover the forking square.
When you are under attack, exchanges reduce the number of attackers. Trading queens often ends an attack on your king at once.

exercises.prompt: Your knight is attacked. You can give a check that also attacks the opponent's queen. What should you do?
options: Give the check: it wins the queen
exercises.explain: The check must be answered, then you take the queen. Winning a queen is worth far more than saving a knight.

exercises.prompt: Your king is on e8 and your rook on a8. An enemy knight sits on b5. Which square is the danger?
exercises.explain: From c7 the knight checks e8 and attacks a8 at the same time.

exercises.prompt: Your opponent has a strong attack against your king. You can trade queens. Should you?
options: Usually yes: the queen is the main attacker
Only if you are losing material

exercises.prompt: Spot the fork before your opponent does: solve these as the attacker.
Find the strongest reply.

lessons.title: Pawn islands and weak pawns
objectives: Count pawn islands
Know the strengths and weaknesses of an isolated pawn
Recognise doubled and backward pawns

steps.say: A group of pawns with no friendly pawns on the files beside it is a pawn island. Fewer islands are usually easier to defend.
An isolated pawn has no friendly pawn on either neighbouring file, so no pawn can defend it. Here White's d-pawn is isolated. It controls central squares but needs pieces to protect it.
Two pawns of the same colour on one file are doubled. They cannot defend each other and the front one blocks the back one.
A backward pawn has fallen behind its neighbours and cannot advance safely. The square in front of it is a hole the opponent can use.

exercises.prompt: How many pawn islands does White have here?
exercises.explain: a-b, d, and f-g-h are three separate groups.

exercises.prompt: What is the square in front of an isolated pawn good for?
options: An outpost for the opponent's pieces
exercises.explain: No pawn can ever chase a piece away from the square in front of an isolated pawn, so it makes a perfect blockade square.

exercises.prompt: Which file has doubled pawns?
Are doubled pawns always bad?
options: No: they can open files and control squares
Only in the endgame they are good

lessons.title: Passed pawns and the rook behind
objectives: Create, push and stop passed pawns
Place rooks behind passed pawns, yours or theirs

steps.say: A passed pawn has no enemy pawns in front of it or on the neighbouring files. Nothing but pieces can stop it, so it grows stronger as pieces come off.
Passed pawns must be pushed. The best way to stop one is to blockade it with a piece directly in front.
A rook behind a passed pawn gains scope as the pawn advances. In front of it, the rook gets boxed in.
The rule works for defence too: put your rook behind the enemy passed pawn.

exercises.prompt: Which white pawn is passed?
Which piece makes the best blockader of a passed pawn?
exercises.explain: A knight is not bothered by standing in front of a pawn and keeps working from there. A queen is too valuable for that job.

exercises.prompt: Where does a rook belong with a passed pawn?
exercises.explain: Tarrasch's rule: rooks belong behind passed pawns, both yours and your opponent's.

exercises.prompt: Why is a rook in front of its own passed pawn passive?
options: Its scope shrinks as the pawn advances

lessons.title: Outposts and weak squares
objectives: Plant a piece where pawns cannot chase it
Find squares your opponent can no longer defend with pawns

steps.say: An outpost is a square in your opponent's half that their pawns can no longer attack. A knight on an outpost, defended by a pawn, can dominate the game.
Here the knight on d5 cannot be driven away by any black pawn. Black must trade a piece for it, often a bishop, to get rid of it.
Pawns cannot move backwards, so every pawn move leaves squares behind that it no longer guards. A hole is a square that no pawn can ever defend.
Holes next to a king are especially dangerous. After g6, the squares f6 and h6 become targets for queens and bishops.

exercises.prompt: Why is d5 a good outpost for the white knight?
options: No black pawn can ever attack it
It is in the centre of the board
It is next to the black king

exercises.prompt: What is the best piece for an outpost?
Why should you think twice before pushing pawns near your king?
options: Each push leaves squares that pawns can never defend again

exercises.prompt: Which piece usually benefits most from a hole in the enemy camp?

lessons.title: Open files and good bishops
objectives: Put rooks on open files
Judge a bishop by its pawns

steps.say: A file with no pawns is open. Rooks belong on open files, where they can reach the seventh rank and attack.
Two rooks on the same open file, doubled, are stronger than one. A rook on the seventh rank attacks pawns and traps the king.
A bishop is bad when its own pawns sit on its colour and block it. Here White's light-squared bishop bites on its own pawns on d5 and e4.
The cure: put your pawns on the opposite colour to your bishop, or trade the bad bishop away.

exercises.prompt: Put a rook on the open d-file.
hints: The d- and e-files have no pawns.
Move one of your rooks there.

exercises.prompt: What is a rook on the seventh rank good for?
options: Attacking pawns and trapping the king

exercises.prompt: Your pawns are on dark squares. Which bishop is likely better?
What are the bishop pair's strengths?
options: They cover both colours and shine in open positions
They are best in closed positions
They can checkmate alone without a king

lessons.title: When to trade and how to convert
objectives: Trade when it helps your plan
Win a won position without risk

steps.say: Every exchange changes the position. Ask: which pieces are good for me, which are good for my opponent? Trade your worst piece for their best.
Trade when you are ahead in material, when you are defending, or when it removes a key defender. Avoid trades when you have more space or the attack.
Once you are ahead, simplify. Trade pieces, not pawns, take away counterplay, and avoid unnecessary risk.
In the endgame, an extra rook mates easily. Push passed pawns, activate your king, and remember to check for stalemate.

exercises.prompt: Which trade is usually good for you?
options: Your bad bishop for their strong knight
Your strong knight for their bad bishop
Your attacking queen when you are attacking

exercises.prompt: You are attacking the enemy king. Your opponent offers a queen trade. Accept?
options: Usually no: the queen is your best attacker
Only if it is a draw

exercises.prompt: You are a piece up. What should you trade?
What is the last thing to check before each move in a winning endgame?
options: That it does not stalemate your opponent
That your king is on the back rank
That you have used your time

lessons.title: Making a plan and stopping theirs
objectives: Find a plan with a simple routine
Stop your opponent's plan before it starts

steps.say: When there are no tactics, ask three questions. What is my worst piece? What is my opponent threatening? Where is their weakness?
Improve the worst piece, stop the threat, then aim at the weakness. Simple plans played well beat clever plans played badly.
Prophylaxis means asking what your opponent wants and preventing it. A quiet move that stops a strong plan is often better than an aggressive one.
A classic example is a pawn move like h3, which stops a bishop or knight from landing on g4.

exercises.prompt: No tactics are on the board. What do you look at first?
Your plan should usually aim at...
options: A weakness in the opponent's position

exercises.prompt: What question leads to prophylactic moves?
options: What does my opponent want to do?
Which piece have I not moved?
How do I win a pawn?

exercises.prompt: Which move stops a black bishop from pinning your knight on f3 from g4?

lessons.title: The initiative and attacking the king
objectives: Keep making threats
Bring more attackers than defenders

steps.say: The side with the initiative makes threats; the other side reacts. Each forcing move keeps the opponent busy and stops their plans.
A pawn or even a piece can be worth giving up if it keeps a strong initiative. But only if the threats keep coming.
An attack succeeds when you have more pieces near the king than your opponent has defending. Count them before you commit.
Opposite-side castling invites pawn storms: push the pawns in front of the enemy king to open files for your rooks.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean to have the initiative?
options: You make threats and your opponent must respond

exercises.prompt: Keep the initiative: find the forcing move.
Before launching an attack on the king, you should...
Finish the attack.
Finish the attack.

lessons.title: Space, active pieces and a whole-game plan
objectives: Gain space with central pawns
Put every piece on its best square
Connect ideas into one game plan

steps.say: Pawns that have crossed into the middle claim space: room behind them for your pieces and less room for your opponent's.
A space advantage means your pieces move freely while your opponent's get in each other's way. Avoid trades when you have more space.
Active pieces control many squares and work together. A knight on the rim controls half as many squares as one in the centre.
In quiet positions, the player who improves pieces fastest usually gets the upper hand.
A good game has a thread: develop and castle, find a weakness, bring pieces to it, trade into a winning endgame.

exercises.prompt: You have more space. Should you trade pieces?
options: Usually not: the cramped side wants trades

exercises.prompt: Which pawns usually give the most space?
options: Centre pawns on the fourth and fifth ranks
Rook pawns on the third rank

exercises.prompt: Which saying is about piece activity?
options: A knight on the rim is dim

exercises.prompt: Which order is a sound game plan?
options: Develop, castle, find a target, attack it, convert
Attack at once with the queen

lessons.title: The active king and the rule of the square
objectives: Bring the king to the centre in the endgame
Tell at a glance if a king can catch a pawn

steps.say: In the middlegame the king hides. In the endgame, with queens gone, it becomes a strong fighting piece. March it to the centre.
The side whose king reaches the centre and the pawns first usually wins the pawn endgame.
Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion rank. If the defending king can step into that square, it catches the pawn.
Here the white king on e1 is one file outside the square a4 to d1, but it is White's move, so it steps into d2 and catches the pawn.

exercises.prompt: Queens have been traded. Where should your king go?
Start centralising your king.
hints: Move the king toward the middle of the board.

exercises.prompt: Black to move. Can the king on g5 catch the pawn on b4?
options: Yes: one step puts it inside the square
No: it is too far away

exercises.prompt: Catch the pawn: step into the square.
hints: The square goes from h4 to e4 to e1 to h1.
Move toward the h-file.

lessons.title: The opposition and king and pawn endings
objectives: Take the opposition to win king and pawn endings
Know which positions win

steps.say: Two kings face each other with one square between them. The side that does not have to move holds the opposition, and the other king must give way.
With the opposition, the attacking king walks around the defender and escorts the pawn home. Without it, the defender holds the draw.
With the king in front of its pawn and the opposition, the pawn usually promotes. With the defending king in front of the pawn, it is usually a draw.
Rook pawns are special: if the defending king reaches the corner, it is always a draw.

exercises.prompt: Kings on d4 and d6, White to move. Who has the opposition?
options: Black: White must move and give way

exercises.prompt: Take the opposition.
hints: Stand right in front of the black king, one square between you.

exercises.prompt: In king and pawn against king, which squares should the attacking king aim for?
options: The key squares two ranks in front of the pawn

exercises.prompt: King and h-pawn against a king in the h8 corner is...
options: A loss for the pawn side

exercises.prompt: Where should the attacking king stand?
options: Far away on the other wing

lessons.title: Rook endings: Lucena and Philidor
objectives: Win the most important rook endgame
Defend rook endings a pawn down

steps.say: Lucena: your pawn is on the seventh, your king in front of it, the enemy king cut off. The winning method is to build a bridge with your rook.
Check to push the enemy king away, bring your rook to the fourth rank, then walk your king out. When the checks come, the rook blocks them.
Philidor: with your king in front of the pawn, keep your rook on the third rank from you to stop the enemy king approaching.
When the pawn advances to the sixth rank, swing your rook behind and check from far away. The king has no shelter.

exercises.prompt: What is the first step in the Lucena position here?
options: Check the black king away from the pawn
Move the king out at once

exercises.prompt: Which rank does the white rook usually go to for the bridge?
In the Philidor position, where does the defending rook wait at first?
options: On the third rank from its own side

exercises.prompt: When the pawn reaches the sixth rank, the defender should...
options: Keep the rook on the third rank

lessons.title: Candidate moves and forcing moves first
objectives: List options before you calculate
Calculate checks and captures first

steps.say: Before you calculate, list two to four candidate moves. Then calculate each in turn. This stops you falling in love with the first idea.
Here, with your queen and bishop aiming at f7, candidates include Qxf7 mate. Always include checks and captures in your list.
Forcing moves leave your opponent few replies, so you can see further. Calculate them first; quiet moves later.
Even if a check does not mate, it might win time, drive a piece away, or set up a fork.

exercises.prompt: Find the best candidate: it is mate.
hints: List every check first.
Your bishop guards g7.

exercises.prompt: How many candidate moves should you usually list?
Look at your checks first.
hints: Look at every queen check.
The back rank is empty.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the forcing line.
Calculate the forcing line.

lessons.title: Seeing ahead and counting exchanges
objectives: Hold a position in your head
Decide whether a capture wins material

steps.say: Calculation means moving the pieces in your head. Start with short lines: your move, their reply, your move. See the final position clearly.
Ask what changed: which squares are attacked now, which pieces are loose? Mistakes in calculation usually come from a piece you forgot had moved.
When several pieces attack one square, count attackers and defenders and their values. Capture with the cheapest piece first.
If you have more attackers than they have defenders, and the trade order does not lose value, the capture wins material.

exercises.prompt: Solve these two-move combinations without moving pieces until you are sure.
Solve these two-move combinations without moving pieces until you are sure.
Most calculation errors come from...
options: Forgetting that a piece has moved

options: Yes, capturing with the knight first
Only if you capture with the rook first

lessons.title: The blunder check and in-between moves
objectives: Check your move before you play it
Look for a stronger move before recapturing

steps.say: Before you touch a piece, look at the board as your opponent: after my move, what are all their checks, captures and threats?
This takes a few seconds and prevents most lost games at every level.
An in-between move, or zwischenzug, is a forcing move played before the expected reply, often a check before recapturing.
Before automatically recapturing, ask: is there a check or a bigger threat first?

exercises.prompt: What is the last thing to do before playing your move?
options: Check every reply your opponent has: checks, captures, threats

exercises.prompt: Spot what your opponent missed.
Spot what your opponent missed.
Your piece was captured. Before recapturing, you should...
options: Look for a check or bigger threat first

exercises.prompt: Find the strongest move, not the obvious one.

lessons.title: Combinations
objectives: Combine motifs into a forcing sequence

steps.say: A combination is a forcing sequence, often with a sacrifice, that ends in a gain. It usually joins two motifs: a deflection and a fork, a check and a pin.
Look for combinations when the opponent's king is exposed, pieces are loose, or pieces are overloaded.
Many combinations begin with a sacrifice. You give up material on purpose, because every reply your opponent has loses even more.

exercises.prompt: Solve the combinations.
Solve the combinations.
Win material with a combination.
Win material with a combination.

lessons.title: Your clock and time trouble
objectives: Spend time where it matters
Play safely when the clock is low

steps.say: Your clock is a resource. Play the opening quickly with known moves; spend time at critical moments: when the position changes, after a capture, or when you sense a tactic.
A useful rule: never let your clock fall far behind your opponent's in a long game. In blitz, keep a few seconds per move in reserve.
In time trouble, simple and safe beats clever. Keep pieces defended, avoid complications, and use checks to gain time.
If your opponent is short of time, keep the position complicated and make them solve problems.

exercises.prompt: When should you think longest?
options: At critical moments: captures, tactics, changes of plan

exercises.prompt: In a game with increment, what does the increment do?
options: Adds time after each move you make

exercises.prompt: You have 20 seconds left in a level position. What kind of moves should you play?
options: Safe, simple moves that keep pieces defended

exercises.prompt: Your opponent is in time trouble. You should...
options: Keep the position complicated but safe for you
Play as fast as possible no matter what

lessons.title: Your openings and your games
objectives: Choose openings you understand
Learn from every game

steps.say: A repertoire is the set of openings you play. Pick a few lines and learn their ideas, not just the moves. The Opening lab helps you drill them.
Start with one answer to 1.e4 and one to 1.d4 as Black, and one first move as White. Expand only when you keep reaching positions you do not understand.
After a game, first look at it on your own and note where you felt unsure. Then use the coach review to check those moments.
Look for patterns across games: the same kind of mistake again and again is your best training target. Your training plan in Improve does this for you.

exercises.prompt: What matters most when learning an opening?
How many openings should a beginner learn first?
options: A small set: one as White and one or two as Black

exercises.prompt: What should you do first after a loss?
options: Review it yourself, then with the coach

exercises.prompt: Which mistakes deserve the most training?
options: The ones you repeat across many games
Opening moves you have never seen

lessons.title: Fair play and a calm mind
objectives: Play fairly and know tournament rules
Stay calm after mistakes

steps.say: Over the board, touch-move applies: if you deliberately touch a piece, you must move it. Say "adjust" first if you only want to straighten it.
Offer draws only on your own move, shake hands before and after, and never use outside help. Online, the same fair-play rules apply.
Everyone blunders. What separates strong players is how they react: reset, look at the new position fresh, and keep fighting.
If you lose several games in a row, take a break. Playing on tilt costs rating and fun. Come back with a puzzle or a lesson instead.

exercises.prompt: Under touch-move, if you touch your knight on purpose you must...
options: Move it if it has a legal move

exercises.prompt: When should you offer a draw over the board?
options: After making your move, before pressing the clock

exercises.prompt: You just blundered a piece. What now?
options: Reset and look for the best move in the new position
Play fast to get it over with

exercises.prompt: You have lost four games in a row. A good next step is...
options: Take a break, then do some puzzles
Raise the time control and keep going angry
